figures.title: The Fat-Soluble Vitamin Family Tree
figures.subtitle: A, D, E and K: four lipids you can’t make enough of.

segments.name: Micronutrients
segments.text: Module 2 is about micronutrients: vitamins and minerals you need in milligrams or micrograms, not grams. They give no calories, but nearly every process in your body depends on them. We start with the four fat-soluble vitamins: A, D, E and K.

segments.name: Four Vitamins
segments.text: Each vitamin across the top links to its own figure. Vitamin A is for vision and growth, D for calcium and bone, E is an antioxidant, and K is needed for blood clotting.

segments.name: Their Forms
segments.text: Each vitamin comes in more than one form. Vitamin A comes ready-made as retinol, or as beta-carotene, which your body converts. D3 comes from skin and animal foods, D2 from fungi. Vitamin E is a family; alpha-tocopherol is the one you need. And K1 comes from plants, K2 from bacteria.
segments.cue: The two rows below, column by column

segments.name: What They Share
segments.text: All four are lipids built from the same five-carbon units, so they dissolve in fat rather than water. They need fat and bile to be absorbed, and they're stored in your liver and fat tissue, so you don't need them every day.

segments.name: Storage Cuts Both Ways
segments.text: Because they build up, large supplement doses of vitamins A and D can be harmful. Food sources almost never cause too much.

figures.title: Built from Isoprene
figures.subtitle: Why these four vitamins dissolve in fat, not water.

segments.name: Isoprene
segments.text: Here's isoprene: five carbons, a four-carbon chain with a one-carbon branch, and two double bonds. Plants and animals join these units head to tail to build long, oily molecules, including cholesterol, carotenoids and all four fat-soluble vitamins.

segments.name: Retinol
segments.text: This is retinol, vitamin A: four isoprene units, twenty carbons. The ring on the left comes from the first unit folded around. The chain has alternating single and double bonds.

segments.name: One OH Is Not Enough
segments.text: Retinol has just one OH group, at the right-hand end. That small water-loving patch is outweighed by thirty hydrogens of oily chain. Compare glucose, with an OH on almost every carbon: glucose dissolves in water, retinol dissolves in fat.

segments.name: Fat- Versus Water-Soluble
segments.text: This table sums up the difference. Fat-soluble vitamins are absorbed with fat into the lymph and stored for weeks to months. Water-soluble vitamins go straight into the blood, and most of any extra leaves in urine.

segments.name: Why It Matters
segments.text: The practical upshot: you can build up stores of fat-soluble vitamins, which protects you through short gaps, but also means megadoses can accumulate to harmful levels.

segments.name: Retinol to Retinal
segments.text: Retinol ends in CH2OH. Take off two hydrogens and it becomes retinal, ending in CH double bond O. Retinal can go on to become retinoic acid, which switches genes on and off for cell growth.

segments.name: How You See
segments.text: Retinal is drawn straight here. In your eye it sits bent at one double bond, inside a protein. When light hits it, it straightens, and that change in shape is the very first step of seeing.

segments.name: What Vitamin A Does
segments.text: Vitamin A is needed for vision, especially in dim light, for healthy skin and the linings of the eyes, gut and lungs, for immune defense, and for growth. Too little causes night blindness and then damage to the eyes; worldwide, it's a leading cause of preventable blindness in children. Too much preformed vitamin A, mostly from supplements, builds up in the liver and can damage it, and in pregnancy can cause birth defects. You find it in liver, fish liver oils, oily fish, eggs and dairy.

segments.name: Beta-Carotene
segments.text: Beta-carotene is the orange pigment in carrots: eight isoprene units, with the same ring at each end. A gut enzyme cuts it in the middle, and each half becomes retinal. That's why it's called provitamin A.

segments.name: Safe from Food
segments.text: Your body only converts beta-carotene as needed, so food sources don't cause vitamin A poisoning. Eating a lot can turn your skin slightly orange, which is harmless. High-dose supplements, though, raised lung cancer risk in smokers in two large trials. Find it in carrots, sweet potato, squash, leafy greens, mango and apricots.

figures.title: Vitamin D
figures.subtitle: Made in your skin from a cholesterol relative, then activated.

segments.name: Made in Your Skin
segments.text: Vitamin D is unusual: your skin can make it. It starts with 7-dehydrocholesterol, which is cholesterol with one extra double bond in the second ring.

segments.name: Sunlight Opens a Ring
segments.text: When UVB light hits the skin, it breaks the second ring open at this bond. With a little body heat, the result is vitamin D3. Count the atoms: same formula, nothing added. Vitamin D is a steroid with a broken ring.

segments.name: D2
segments.text: Vitamin D2 is almost identical: one extra double bond and one extra carbon in the tail. Fungi and yeast make it from their own sterol when exposed to UV light.

segments.name: Activation
segments.text: Neither form does anything yet. The liver adds an OH to make 25-hydroxyvitamin D, the form a blood test measures. Then the kidney adds a second OH, making calcitriol, the active hormone. Calcitriol raises calcium and phosphate absorption from the gut and keeps bones mineralized.

segments.name: Needs and Sources
segments.text: The RDA is fifteen micrograms, six hundred units, a day for ages one to seventy, and twenty micrograms over seventy. Too little causes soft bones: rickets in children, osteomalacia in adults. Too much, only from supplements, raises blood calcium. Few foods have much: oily fish, cod liver oil, egg yolks, and UV-exposed mushrooms. That's why milk is often fortified.

figures.title: Vitamin E
figures.subtitle: The tocopherols, and how they protect cell membranes.

segments.name: Alpha-Tocopherol
segments.text: Here's alpha-tocopherol, the main form of vitamin E. It has a two-ring head carrying an OH group and three methyl groups, and a long sixteen-carbon tail.

segments.name: Head and Tail
segments.text: The tail anchors the molecule inside fatty cell membranes. The OH on the head is the working part: it can give up its hydrogen to stop a chain reaction of damage.

segments.name: Alpha Versus Gamma
segments.text: Gamma-tocopherol is the same except for one methyl group on the ring, replaced by a plain hydrogen. It's actually the most common form in the US diet, from soybean and corn oils. But the liver keeps only the alpha form in the blood, so only alpha counts toward your needs.

segments.name: Stopping a Chain Reaction
segments.text: Polyunsaturated fats in membranes are easily damaged. A reactive oxygen molecule steals a hydrogen from one, which then attacks its neighbor, and so on. Vitamin E hands over a hydrogen and stops the chain. Vitamin C helps restore it afterwards.

segments.name: Needs and Sources
segments.text: The RDA is fifteen milligrams of alpha-tocopherol a day. Deficiency is rare, mostly in people who can't absorb fat, and causes nerve and muscle damage. Supplements above the upper limit, a thousand milligrams a day, raise bleeding risk. The best sources are sunflower seeds, almonds, hazelnuts, wheat germ, and sunflower and safflower oils.

figures.title: Vitamin K
figures.subtitle: Two forms, one working head: clotting and bone.

segments.name: The Working Head
segments.text: Every form of vitamin K has the same head: a double ring with two C double bond O groups. That head does the chemistry.

segments.name: K1 and K2
segments.text: What differs is the tail. K1, phylloquinone, made by plants in their leaves, has a mostly saturated tail. K2, the menaquinones, have tails that keep a double bond in every isoprene unit. MK-4 has four units; bacteria make longer ones, like MK-7 in natto.
segments.cue: Marker 2 on K1, then K2, marker 3

segments.name: Clotting
segments.text: The liver makes several clotting proteins in an inactive form. Vitamin K helps add an extra acid group to some of their amino acids, which lets them hold calcium and gather at a wound to form a clot. The same change activates calcium-binding proteins in bone.

segments.name: Newborns
segments.text: Very little vitamin K crosses the placenta and breast milk is low in it, so newborns get a vitamin K injection at birth to prevent bleeding. In adults, deficiency is rare.

segments.name: Needs and Sources
segments.text: The adequate intake is a hundred and twenty micrograms a day for men and ninety for women. No harm is known from high intakes. But people taking the blood thinner warfarin are advised to keep their vitamin K intake steady, because it counteracts the drug. K1 is in kale, spinach, collards, broccoli and soybean and canola oils; K2 in natto, cheese and egg yolks.

figures.title: Absorption, Storage and Labels
figures.subtitle: How they get in, where they are kept, and the forms on labels.

segments.name: With Fat
segments.text: Fat-soluble vitamins are absorbed far better with a little fat in the same meal. Bile mixes them into tiny droplets, the gut wall packs them into chylomicrons with the fat, and they travel through the lymph before reaching the blood and liver.

segments.name: Where They Are Stored
segments.text: Vitamin A is stored mainly in the liver; D and E in fat tissue and the liver. Vitamin K is used up fastest.

segments.name: Forms on the Label
segments.text: On ingredient lists you'll see vitamin A as retinyl palmitate or acetate, or as beta-carotene, which is also used as a color. D3 is cholecalciferol and D2 ergocalciferol. Natural vitamin E is d-alpha-tocopherol; the synthetic dl- form has about half the activity. Tocopherols are also added to oils as antioxidants, as E306 to E309.

segments.name: Daily Values
segments.text: The Daily Values are nine hundred micrograms of vitamin A, twenty micrograms of D, fifteen milligrams of E, and a hundred and twenty micrograms of K. Since the 2016 update, US labels must list vitamin D; A, E and K appear only if added or claimed.

figures.title: Where fat-soluble vitamins are used in the body
figures.subtitle: Tap a number on the cell to see what that part does; the list below it gives every other place in the body.

segments.name: Where Vitamins A, D, E and K Go
segments.text: Here's where the fat-soluble vitamins are used or stored: first inside a single cell, then everywhere else in the body. Because they dissolve in fat, they're absorbed with fat and can be stored, mostly in the liver and fat tissue.
segments.cue: The cell drawing and the list of places

segments.name: Inside a Cell
segments.text: Fat-soluble vitamins live where the fat is. Vitamin E guards the membrane against oxidation. Vitamins A and D, once activated, go right into the nucleus and change which genes are read. Vitamin K works in the rough ER, finishing clotting proteins so they can grab calcium. And vitamin A is stored for months in fat droplets in liver cells.

foodBody.name: Vitamin A
foodBody.text: Retinol from liver, eggs and dairy; beta-carotene from orange and green vegetables is turned into it.

foodBody.name: Vitamin D
foodBody.text: Made in skin from sunlight, or from fatty fish and fortified foods; it needs two activation steps.

foodBody.name: Vitamin K
foodBody.text: K1 from leafy greens, K2 from fermented foods and some made by gut bacteria.

segments.name: Vitamin A
segments.text: In the eye, vitamin A becomes retinal, the part of rhodopsin that catches light, so a shortage causes night blindness first. It also keeps the skin and the linings of the gut and lungs healthy. The liver stores most of your vitamin A.
segments.cue: In the list: eyes, liver and skin

foodBody.name: Retinol and beta-carotene
foodBody.text: Retinol comes from liver, eggs and dairy; beta-carotene from carrots, sweet potatoes and leafy greens, and your gut turns it into vitamin A. In the eye it becomes retinal.

segments.name: Vitamin D
segments.text: The skin makes vitamin D in sunlight. The liver turns it into its blood form, and the kidneys into calcitriol, the active hormone. Calcitriol helps the small intestine absorb calcium for the bones.
segments.cue: In the list: skin, liver, kidneys, small intestine and bones

foodBody.name: Vitamin D
foodBody.text: Oily fish, egg yolks and fortified milk give some, but most people get much of theirs from sunlight on the skin. In the body it works as a hormone that controls calcium.

segments.name: Vitamins E and K
segments.text: Vitamin E sits in cell membranes and protects them from oxidation; fat tissue holds most of the store. Vitamin K lets the liver make clotting factors, so blood can clot, and it also activates proteins in bone.
segments.cue: In the list: bones, fat tissue and blood

foodBody.name: Vitamin E
foodBody.text: Nuts, seeds and plant oils such as sunflower oil. In the body it is an antioxidant in membranes.

foodBody.name: Vitamin K
foodBody.text: Leafy greens give K1; fermented foods and gut bacteria give some K2. In the body it activates clotting factors and bone proteins.

segments.name: Simplified
segments.text: This is simplified. Vitamin A and vitamin D act in many tissues, so the list gives each place's main job, not every detail.

figures.title: Putting It All Together
figures.subtitle: The whole lesson in one table, plus a few extras.

segments.name: One Table
segments.text: Here are the four fat-soluble vitamins in one table: their main forms, what they do, what happens with too little or too much, and where to find them in whole foods.

segments.name: Worth Knowing
segments.text: A few extras. Eat colorful vegetables with a little fat to absorb their carotenoids and vitamin K. Liver is so rich in vitamin A that it's best eaten occasionally, especially in pregnancy. Sunlight can't give you too much vitamin D, but supplements can. And these vitamins are close relatives of cholesterol, built from the same isoprene units. Try the quiz below.
